title: India Forex Reserves Surge to $692.9 Billion on Record FCNR Inflows
excerpt: Reserves posted their biggest weekly jump in six months, buoyed by $36.7 billion in foreign currency deposits from NRIs as the RBI holds rates steady at 5.25%.
body:
• India's foreign exchange reserves rose to $692.9 billion as of July 31, their highest level in nearly three months, jumping $10.5 billion in a single week
  • The surge was driven by $36.7 billion in Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits mobilized under the RBI's concessional swap scheme launched in June
  • The RBI held its repo rate at 5.25% on August 5, voting unanimously to stand pat as it assesses inflationary pressures from the Iran war and elevated oil prices
  • Reserves remain well below the all-time high of $728.5 billion hit in February, but analysts expect them to cross $700 billion in coming weeks

India's foreign exchange reserves surged to a near three-month high of $692.9 billion as of July 31, powered by an aggressive foreign currency deposit drive that has pulled in tens of billions of dollars from non-resident Indians, Reserve Bank of India data showed this week.

The $10.5 billion weekly jump was the largest since the week ended January 30, underscoring the success of the RBI's campaign to shore up the country's balance of payments at a time when oil price volatility from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continues to strain India's external accounts.

FCNR Deposits Drive the Buildup

The bulk of the inflows came through the RBI's concessional foreign exchange swap facility, launched on June 8 to attract fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank (FCNR-B) deposits. Under the scheme, commercial banks can raise dollar-denominated deposits from NRIs and swap them with the central bank at zero hedging cost. The facility runs through September 30 for FCNR deposits and December 31 for overseas borrowings.

As of July 31, the facility had drawn $40.8 billion in total inflows: $36.7 billion through FCNR-B deposits, $2.6 billion via Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings, and $1.5 billion through External Commercial Borrowings, according to RBI data. SBI Economic Research expects FCNR deposits alone to reach $65-70 billion by the scheme's end, with total inflows of $80-85 billion — far surpassing the $26 billion mobilized under a similar 2013 initiative.

"As flows from the FCNR scheme have gained pace, we expect the headline FX reserve figure to cross $700 billion in coming weeks, and it will also help the RBI to reduce its short FX book."

— Dhaval Shah, Founder and MD, De-Risk Forex Consultancy

RBI Holds Rates, Signals Patience

The reserves data came days after the RBI's monetary policy committee voted unanimously on August 5 to hold the repo rate at 5.25%, maintaining its neutral stance. Governor Sanjay Malhotra said headline inflation had moved above the 4% target mainly because of fuel prices, while broader price pressures remained in check.

The central bank trimmed its full-year inflation forecast to 5.0% from 5.1% and cut its core inflation projection — excluding food and fuel — to 4.3% from 4.7%. Malhotra said reserves were "adequate" with import cover of over 10 months and external debt cover of 90.8%.

The decision to hold rates contrasts with several emerging-market peers, including Indonesia and the Philippines, that have raised borrowing costs to counter inflation and currency depreciation driven by elevated energy prices.

Rupee Stabilizes but Upside Limited

The rupee gained 1.2% during the week to 95.38 per dollar, its biggest weekly advance in four months, reflecting both the reserve buildup and broader dollar weakness. But analysts cautioned that lasting appreciation is unlikely.

The RBI's outstanding forward dollar commitments exceed $100 billion, meaning a large portion of the incoming flows will be needed to settle existing obligations rather than actively strengthen the currency. A Reuters poll of 36 strategists projected the rupee largely flat at 95.25 per dollar in three months, weakening slightly to 95.95 in a year.

"Inflows will be enough to fund the RBI's requirements rather than be used for currency appreciation. I expect more sideways movement for the rupee rather than any upside."

— Anitha Rangan, Chief Economist, RBL Bank

What It Means for NRI Depositors

The FCNR scheme represents a rare alignment of interests for NRI savers. Banks are offering competitive rates on dollar-denominated deposits, while the RBI's zero-cost swap backstop removes the currency hedging risk that typically eats into NRI deposit returns. Public-sector banks have been the primary drivers of mobilization, with outreach intensifying across key markets in the Gulf, the U.S., and the U.K.

Reserves remain well below the all-time high of $728.5 billion reached in February, before the onset of the Middle East conflict. But with the FCNR pipeline still accelerating and deposits maturing in August and September likely to be renewed under the new scheme, analysts expect the $700 billion threshold to be reclaimed within weeks.
nri_angle: The RBI's FCNR deposit scheme offers NRI savers competitive dollar-denominated returns with zero hedging cost, directly benefiting diaspora investors.
author: Diaspora Desk
